title: Earth-Agent: Unlocking the Full Landscape of Earth Observation with Agents
one_liner: Give an Earth observation agent access to domain tools across image types so it can answer scientific questions that require several measured steps, not just one visual guess.
lead: Earth observation work rarely ends with one image caption. Scientists need to compare dates, combine sensor types, extract measured quantities, and call specialist tools that know how to turn raw satellite data into usable estimates. General vision-language systems are weak at this because they usually focus on visible-color images and short responses. Earth-Agent builds an agent framework for this domain. It combines visible-color and spectral data inside one tool ecosystem and evaluates the whole process with a benchmark that checks both the reasoning path and the final answer. The goal is not only to describe what an image shows, but to answer real scientific questions by invoking the right tools in sequence.

problem.h2: Why ordinary vision agents are too shallow for Earth observation
paras: A remote-sensing question may ask for crop stress over time, water change across regions, or a physical quantity derived from multiple sensor bands. A standard image agent often answers from one picture and one pass of text generation. That is too shallow for scientific use because the question may require comparing several dates, calling a retrieval tool, applying a domain model, and checking units before answering.

There is also a modality gap. Earth data does not come only as visible-color images. It includes spectral measurements and derived products whose meaning depends on domain-specific processing. An agent that only reads ordinary pictures cannot use much of the evidence scientists rely on.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Unify visible-color imagery, spectral data, and specialist Earth tools in one agent loop so multi-step scientific questions can be solved through tool use.

steps.text: The question may ask for comparison across dates, sensor types, or physical quantities.
The agent selects visible-color imagery, spectral data, derived products, or several of them together.
It invokes specialist tools to retrieve scenes, calculate quantities, or compare locations and times.
The system keeps the measured results from each tool call so later steps can build on them.
The final response uses the tool outputs rather than only a free-form visual guess.

paras: The paper changes the capability boundary of the agent. Instead of one model looking at one picture, the agent can coordinate multiple Earth data types and domain tools inside a single reasoning loop.
object.object: the agent's access to domain modalities and tools

hidden.name: How much of a real Earth workflow the agent can execute
paras: The important quantity is scientific reach: the fraction of domain work the agent can carry out before a human must take over. A system with low reach may answer basic visible-color questions but fail as soon as the task needs spectral analysis, measured outputs, or multi-date comparison.

Earth-Agent raises this quantity by extending the tool and data space. The benchmark makes that visible by including tasks over visible-color imagery, spectral inputs, and derived products, then scoring both the action path and the final answer. That matters because a final answer can look plausible even when the intermediate tool use was wrong.

heat.caption: Darker means the task demands more of a real Earth analysis workflow and is better served by tool-based reasoning.

reads.html: Scientific reach asks how far the agent can get through a real remote-sensing task before it runs out of data access, tool access, or multi-step reasoning.
Earth-Bench evaluates spectrum, products, and visible-color tasks with dual-level scoring so both trajectory quality and final outcome count.

mechanism.h2: Why the tool ecosystem matters more than one stronger captioning model
paras: A stronger captioning model can describe imagery more fluently, but that alone does not produce quantitative Earth analysis because scientific tasks need explicit operations: retrieve the right scene, compute a domain quantity, align time points, compare locations, and check the result. Earth-Agent gives the model a way to call those operations directly.

This changes the system from a one-shot predictor into a workflow controller. The answer improves because each step can use the right data type and the right specialist tool. Visible-color inputs can support broad scene understanding, while spectral inputs and derived products support measured conclusions. The benchmark's trajectory scoring is important because it rewards correct scientific process, not just a plausible sentence at the end.

math.words: Score both whether the final answer is right and whether the intermediate tool sequence followed a sound scientific path.
symbols: credit for using a sensible sequence of domain tools and intermediate steps
credit for the final task answer
combined evaluation across process and outcome

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: A task asks for a quantity change between two dates.
The agent retrieves both scenes, runs the needed domain tool, and compares the resulting values.
Suppose the tool path is mostly correct, so path_score = 0.8.
Suppose the final numeric answer is also correct, so answer_score = 1.0.
If the final answer had looked plausible but the tool sequence was unsound, path_score would fall, exposing the weakness.

math.note: Dual-level scoring matters because scientific credibility depends on process as well as outcome.

charts.title: General image agent
charts.note: Ordinary visual agents can describe scenes but struggle when the task needs domain tools and measured reasoning.

charts.title: Earth-Agent
charts.note: Earth-Agent expands capability because it combines modalities and tool use in one loop.

items.html: If the agent chooses a tool for the wrong sensor type or quantity, the rest of the workflow can stay internally neat but still answer the wrong question.

items.b: Intermediate measurements are not carried forward correctly.
items.html: Multi-step Earth tasks depend on earlier outputs. If one value is dropped or misread, later comparison steps can fail even when the right tools were called.
A scientific answer can sound reasonable while resting on a flawed process. That is why the benchmark scores the path as well as the endpoint.

When the agent selects the right modality, calls the right domain tools, and preserves intermediate results, it can solve harder Earth tasks because the workflow mirrors how domain experts actually work.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a benchmark slice with tasks over visible-color imagery, spectral data, and multi-date comparison. Compare a plain image-question-answering system against an agent that can call retrieval and quantity-estimation tools. The tool-based system should win on questions that require measured outputs and several steps because those tasks exceed what one visual pass can support.
demo.closing: The demo should make clear that real Earth analysis depends on workflow control, not only image description.
